blocks.rendered_text: 2 Preliminaries We write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm and $I_{d}$ for the $d\times d$ identity matrix. For symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$ , the notation $A\preceq B$ means that $B-A$ is positive semidefinite. Let $O(n):=\{O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:O^{\top}O=I_{n}\}$ denote the real orthogonal group, equipped with Haar probability measure. It has two components, $\{\det O=+1\}$ , $\{\det O=-1\}$ , and each have Haar probability $1/2$ . For $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ , we write $\mu_{n,b}$ for Haar probability measure conditioned on $\det O=b$ . Targets and oracle. We restrict the target class to centered Gaussians. This restriction removes the hardness of locating the target and isolates the difficulty of sampling with an unknown covariance. For an integer $d\geq 1$ and a parameter $\kappa\geq 1$ , without loss of generality, we normalize the spectral bounds to $1$ and $\kappa$ by rescaling and consider the precision class $\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}:=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:A=A^{\top},\quad I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}\right\}.$ An input $A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}$ specifies the quadratic potential $f_{A}(x):=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax$ and the target distribution $\pi_{A}:=N(0,A^{-1})$ . At a point $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the exact first-order oracle returns $\operatorname{FO}_{A}(x):=\bigl(f_{A}(x),\nabla f_{A}(x)\bigr)=\left(\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax,Ax\right).$ (1) On this class, exact first-order access is equivalent to exact matrix–vector access. Indeed, a first-order response contains $Ax$ , while a matrix–vector response determines both the gradient $Ax$ and the function value $\frac{1}{2}\langle x,Ax\rangle$ . Thus the exact value-and-gradient, gradient-only, and matrix–vector query complexities coincide. Randomized algorithms. A randomized algorithm chooses its queries and stopping decisions as Borel functions of its internal randomness and previous oracle responses, where the randomness is independent of the input. Its output may be any $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ -valued Borel function of the same information. The algorithm has fixed query budget $T$ if it makes at most $T$ queries for every admissible input and every realization of its internal randomness. Accuracy measures. For probability measures $P$ and $Q$ on a common measurable space, their total variation distance is $\operatorname{TV}(P,Q):=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\int|p-q|\,d\lambda,$ where the supremum ranges over measurable sets, and $p$ and $q$ are the densities of $P$ and $Q$ with respect to any common dominating measure $\lambda$ . In particular, $|\mathbb{E}_{P}h-\mathbb{E}_{Q}h|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)$ for every measurable function $h$ taking values in $[0,1]$ . Sampling accuracy and query complexity. For a fixed input $A$ , let $\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}$ denote the law of the algorithm’s output, with all internal randomness included. For $0<\varepsilon<1$ , define $Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon):=\inf\left\{T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{Alg}\text{ with fixed query budget }T\\[2.0pt] \text{such that }\displaystyle\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}}\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A}\bigr)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}.$ (2) The accuracy requirement is uniform over inputs and concerns the output law after averaging over the algorithm’s seed. Throughout the paper, query budgets are deterministic caps on the number of queries in each run, rather than bounds on the expected number of queries.

blocks.rendered_text: Theorem 4.1 ( Extension to general $\kappa$ ). For every fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ , there exists $d_{0}(\delta)$ such that, for every integer $d\geq d_{0}(\delta)$ , $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ , and $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ , $Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{\delta}{256}\sqrt{\kappa}\log d.$

Compared with Theorem 3.1 , this bound also covers $2\leq\kappa<4$ and $\frac{1}{16}<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{10}$ , and it holds even when the spectrum of $A$ is known to the algorithm. On the other hand, it does not grow as $\varepsilon\to 0$ and it requires $\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ .

blocks.rendered_text: 4.1 The Hard Family We use a construction similar to that in [ 22 , Section 9.2] , with a cosine eigenvalue grid (Chebyshev nodes) and a random orthogonal rotation, while extending the spectral interval from $[1,2]$ to $[1,\kappa]$ . For $d\geq 2$ and $\kappa\geq 2$ , define $\theta_{i}=\frac{(i-\tfrac{1}{2})\pi}{d},\qquad\lambda_{i}=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}+\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\cos\theta_{i},\qquad\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}).$ (11) Draw $O\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathrm{O}(d))$ , independently of the algorithm’s private randomness, and set $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ . The associated potential and target are $f_{A}(x)=x^{\top}Ax/2$ and $\pi_{A}=N(0,A^{-1})$ . The spectrum is deterministic and may be supplied to the algorithm. In particular, the Gaussian normalizing constant is known. The unknown component is the random eigenbasis represented by $O$ . Remark 4.2 ( Comparison with $\kappa=2$ case). At $\kappa=2$ , the spectrum in Eq. ( 11 ) recovers the original construction in [ 22 ] . More generally, if $A_{2}$ denotes the original precision matrix with the same rotation $O$ , then $A=(\kappa-1)A_{2}-(\kappa-2)I_{d}$ . Thus one matrix–vector reply for either matrix determines the corresponding reply for the other. The proof compares $\sum_{i}\cos(n\theta_{i})\langle x,Oe_{i}\rangle^{2}$ with $\|x\|^{2}$ , where $n=2q+1$ . For the output of a $q$ -query algorithm, the ratio is at most $d^{-\Omega(1)}$ in absolute value (Lemma 4.4 ), whereas under the target the ratio of the means has absolute value $e^{-\Theta(n/\sqrt{\kappa})}$ (Lemma 4.5 ). Hence the test works for $n$ up to order $\sqrt{\kappa}\log d$ , rather than $\log d$ as at $\kappa=2$ , which is the source of the factor $\sqrt{\kappa}$ in Theorem 4.1 .

blocks.rendered_text: 4.2 Properties of the Hard Family This subsection states the four lemmas used in the proof of Theorem 4.1 . Lemma 4.3 places the output of any $q$ -query algorithm in a block Krylov space generated by independent Gaussian vectors, Lemma 4.4 bounds a quadratic form with cosine weights uniformly over this space, Lemma 4.5 evaluates the same quadratic form under the target, and Lemma 4.6 verifies that the hard family is admissible. All proofs are deferred to Appendix C . Krylov representation of the output. We first control the information revealed by adaptive queries via a standard Krylov argument. The deferred-rotation argument of [ 22 , Lemma 9.2] uses the rotational symmetry of the undisclosed eigenbasis to represent the algorithm’s output in a block Krylov space generated by independent Gaussian vectors. For vectors $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d})$ , define $\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})=\operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^{j}g_{a}:1\leq a\leq q+1,\ 0\leq j\leq q\}.$ Lemma 4.3 ( Krylov representation). Fix an integer $q\geq 0$ with $2q+1<d$ and let $X$ be the output. There exist independent vectors $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\sim N(0,I_{d})$ such that $O^{\top}X\in\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})\qquad\text{almost surely}.$ The additional starting vector accounts for the output, which may lie outside the span of the query points and oracle replies. Equivalently, the lemma gives a representation $O^{\top}X=\sum_{a=1}^{q+1}p_{a}(\Lambda)g_{a}$ , where each $p_{a}$ has degree at most $q$ . The polynomial coefficients may depend on the entire extended experiment. We therefore control the output through an estimate that holds simultaneously for every vector in $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ . The proof of Lemma 4.3 is deferred to Appendix C.1 . A uniform bound on the Krylov space. We next control a high-frequency cosine statistic uniformly over the space in Lemma 4.3 . For a query budget $q$ , set $n=2q+1,\qquad D_{n}=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\cos(n\theta_{1}),\ldots,\cos(n\theta_{d})\bigr).$ The choice of $n$ places this statistic above all frequencies arising from products of two degree- $q$ cosine polynomials. Lemma 4.4 ( Uniform bound on the Krylov space). There is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that the following holds. Let $q\geq 0$ satisfy $2q+1<d$ , let $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}$ be independent $N(0,I_{d})$ vectors, and let $\mathcal{K}_{q}=\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})$ . Define $\tau_{d,q}=C\left[(q+1)\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{d}}+\frac{(q+1)(q+1+\log d)\log d}{d}\right].$ If $\tau_{d,q}\leq 1/2$ , then, with probability at least $0.99$ , $|u^{\top}D_{n}u|\leq 2\tau_{d,q}\|u\|^{2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal{K}_{q}.$ The proof is deferred to Appendix C.2 . Since $\lambda_{i}$ is a nonconstant affine function of $\cos\theta_{i}$ , the space $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ is equivalently spanned by the vectors $\bigl((g_{a})_{i}\cos(j\theta_{i})\bigr)_{i=1}^{d}$ , with $a\leq q+1$ and $j\leq q$ . Consequently, the estimate is independent of $\kappa$ . On the event in Lemma 4.4 , the output representation in Lemma 4.3 therefore gives $\bigl|X^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}X\bigr|\leq 2\tau_{d,q}\|X\|^{2}.$ Target moments. We now evaluate the same cosine statistic under the target Gaussian. Lemma 4.5 ( Moments under the target). Let $\kappa\geq 2$ , $U\sim N(0,\Lambda^{-1})$ , and $\varrho_{\kappa}=\tfrac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}$ . For an integer $1\leq n<d$ , put $D_{n}=\operatorname{diag}(\cos(n\theta_{i}))$ , $M=\mathbb{E}\|U\|^{2}$ , and $\mu_{n}=\mathbb{E}[U^{\top}D_{n}U]$ . Then $\displaystyle M$ $\displaystyle=\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{1-\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}}{1+\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}},\quad\mbox{and }(-1)^{n}\mu_{n}=\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{\varrho_{\kappa}^{n}-\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d-n}}{1+\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}}.$ Moreover, both $\operatorname{Var}(\|U\|^{2})$ and $\operatorname{Var}(U^{\top}D_{n}U)$ are at most $2M\leq 2d/\sqrt{\kappa}$ . If $d-n\geq\sqrt{\kappa}$ , then $(1-e^{-4})e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq\frac{|\mu_{n}|}{M}\leq e^{-2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}.$ The proof is deferred to Appendix C.3 . For an exact sample $Y\mid O\sim\pi_{A}$ , the vector $U=O^{\top}Y$ has law $N(0,\Lambda^{-1})$ , with $\|Y\|^{2}=\|U\|^{2}$ and $Y^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}Y=U^{\top}D_{n}U$ . The lemma therefore gives the means and variances of $\|Y\|^{2}$ and $Y^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}Y$ under the target. Admissibility and oracle equivalence. We finally verify that the hard family belongs to the prescribed class. The proof is deferred to Appendix C.4 . Lemma 4.6 ( Admissibility). For every $O\in\mathrm{O}(d)$ , the matrix $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ satisfies $I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}$ .

blocks.rendered_text: C.4 Proof of Lemma 4.6 Proof of Lemma 4.6 . Since $0<\theta_{i}<\pi$ , we have $-1<\cos\theta_{i}<1$ , and hence $1<\lambda_{i}<\kappa$ . As $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ with $O$ orthogonal, this gives $I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}$ . The potential $V_{A}(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax$ is $C^{\infty}$ with Hessian $\nabla^{2}V_{A}(x)=A$ . Thus it is $1$ -strongly convex and $\kappa$ -smooth. Moreover, $V_{A}(0)=0$ and $V_{A}(x)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\|x\|^{2}>0$ for $x\neq 0$ , so $0$ is its unique minimizer. The associated target is $N(0,A^{-1})$ . Gaussian integration gives $Z_{A}=(2\pi)^{d/2}(\det A)^{-1/2}=(2\pi)^{d/2}(\det\Lambda)^{-1/2}.$ Since $\Lambda$ is fixed, $Z_{A}$ is independent of $O$ and is known whenever the spectrum is public. ∎

blocks.rendered_text: 4.4 Limitations of the Analysis Theorem 4.1 is restricted to $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ for fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ . Although it applies to every $\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ , its lower bound does not grow as $\varepsilon$ decreases. We discuss two limitations of the analysis that affect extensions to larger condition numbers and higher accuracy. Limitation on $\kappa$ . Our approach does not extend the $\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ lower bound to condition numbers $\kappa\gtrsim d/\log^{2}d$ . Our proof controls the output of the algorithm by first applying Lemma 4.3 to place $O^{\top}X$ in $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ , and then bounding the cosine statistic uniformly over this space. However, the enlarged space $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ has $(q+1)^{2}$ generating vectors. Since the eigenvalues of $\Lambda$ are distinct, these vectors span a space of the following dimension. Lemma 4.7 ( Dimension of the Krylov space). For every integer $q\geq 0$ and independent $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\allowbreak\sim N(0,I_{d})$ , $\dim\mathcal{K}_{q}=\min\{d,(q+1)^{2}\}\qquad\text{almost surely}.$ Once $(q+1)^{2}\geq d$ with $q=\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ , we have $\mathcal{K}_{q}=\mathbb{R}^{d}$ almost surely. For $n=2q+1<d$ , the definition of $\theta_{i}$ gives $\sum_{i}^{d}\cos^{2}(n\theta_{i})=d/2$ , so at least one coordinate satisfies $|\cos(n\theta_{i})|\geq 1/\sqrt{2}$ . Taking its coordinate unit vector yields $\sup_{u\in\mathcal{K}_{q}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|u^{\top}D_{n}u|}{\|u\|^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Our separating test in Lemma 4.4 requires this supremum to be at most $1/2$ , which is incompatible with the displayed bound. Thus an argument based on a uniform bound over $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ cannot apply once $(q+1)^{2}\geq d$ . Limitation on accuracy. Our test compares the ratio $(-1)^{n}x^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}x/\|x\|^{2}$ with a threshold $t$ . Lemma 4.4 puts every output of the algorithm below $t$ only if $t\geq a$ , where $a$ is the uniform bound on $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ that the lemma provides. Chebyshev’s inequality with Lemma 4.5 puts samples from the target above $t$ only if $t<|\mu_{n}|/M$ . Thus $|\mu_{n}|/M>a$ , whatever the threshold. At the same time, the Bernstein calculation in the proof of Fact C.6 requires $a\geq c/\sqrt{d}$ even to certify a failure probability below one. Finally, Lemma 4.5 gives $|\mu_{n}|/M\leq e^{-2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}$ . Since $n=2q+1$ , we must have $\frac{c}{\sqrt{d}}\leq a<\frac{|\mu_{n}|}{M}\leq e^{-2(2q+1)/\sqrt{\kappa}}.$ Taking logarithms yields $q=O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ , independently of $\varepsilon$ . A different choice of the threshold or of the constants therefore cannot give a bound that grows as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . Remark 4.8 ( Scope of the limitations). These limitations concern our proof. We do not know whether the same fixed-spectrum family supports stronger lower bounds. Our analysis therefore leaves open whether the same fixed-spectrum family supports stronger lower bounds.
